name: webanno.custom.Statement
description: A conclusion, premise or lever. Its role comes from the connectors linking it. Implicit statements are zero-width (Shift+click) with their wording in note. E.g. in 'Socrates is a man; therefore he is mortal': 'Socrates is a man', 'he is mortal' (note: Socrates is mortal), and a zero-width 'All men are mortal'.

features.name: note
features.description: Doubts, the label you nearly chose, or the wording of an implicit statement.

name: webanno.custom.Connector
description: One PTA argument: one conclusion, one premise, one lever. Anchor on the coherence marker (because, so, …), or zero-width if there is none. E.g. on 'therefore' in 'Socrates is a man; therefore he is mortal': conclusion 'he is mortal', premise the implicit 'All men are mortal', lever statement 'Socrates is a man'; beta, β su, GENUS.

features.name: form
features.description: Which elements conclusion and premise share.

tags.tag_description: a is X because a is Y: same subject, different predicates. E.g. the minister did a great job because the minister raised the budget.
a is X because b is X: same predicate, different subjects. E.g. Socrates is mortal because all men are mortal.
a is X because b is Y: nothing shared. E.g. peace can be started by truth because war can be started by lies.
q is A/U because q is Z: the premise says something about the conclusion as a whole (who says it, what follows from it). E.g. the economy grew [is acceptable] because Eurostat says so.

features.name: substance
features.description: Prefixed with the form; conclusion first, then premise.

features.name: conclusion
features.description: The statement argued for. Exactly one. E.g. 'Socrates is mortal'.

features.name: premise
features.description: The reason given; when two statements support jointly, the one the text marks as the reason, else the generalization. Exactly one. E.g. 'all men are mortal'.

features.name: leverStatement
features.description: The lever as a statement, only if the text states it or argues about it; otherwise leave empty (the lever keyword is enough). At most one. E.g. 'Socrates is a man' (membership), 'robots are just like us' (likeness).

features.name: conclusionSubject
features.description: The conclusion's subject in canonical form: a in the lever templates; for delta, the whole proposition q. E.g. 'Socrates'.

features.name: conclusionPredicate
features.description: The conclusion's predicate in canonical form: X in the lever templates; for delta, '[is acceptable]' or '[is unacceptable]' (A/U). E.g. 'is mortal'.

features.name: premiseSubject
features.description: The premise's subject in canonical form: b in the lever templates (a again for alpha); for delta, q. E.g. 'all men'.

features.name: premisePredicate
features.description: The premise's predicate in canonical form: Y in the lever templates (X again for beta); for delta, Z. E.g. 'are mortal'.

features.name: transformations
features.description: The transformations that changed a subject's or predicate's wording, each with the statement it applied to; once each, in any order. Empty if the text needed none.

tags.tag_description: A reference replaced by what it refers to. E.g. 'it' -> 'unauthorized downloading'. Applied to the conclusion.
A reference replaced by what it refers to. E.g. 'it' -> 'unauthorized downloading'. Applied to the premise.
Implicit content made explicit. E.g. 'why should you?' -> 'why should you stop carrying guns?'. Applied to the conclusion.
Implicit content made explicit. E.g. 'why should you?' -> 'why should you stop carrying guns?'. Applied to the premise.
A rhetorical question (or other illocution) turned into an assertion. E.g. 'why should you?' -> 'you should not'. Applied to the conclusion.
A rhetorical question (or other illocution) turned into an assertion. E.g. 'why should you?' -> 'you should not'. Applied to the premise.
Active turned passive to bring out a shared term. E.g. 'many people have said q' -> 'q has been said by many people'. Applied to the conclusion.
Active turned passive to bring out a shared term. E.g. 'many people have said q' -> 'q has been said by many people'. Applied to the premise.
Passive turned active to bring out a shared term. E.g. 'the budget was raised by the minister' -> 'the minister raised the budget'. Applied to the conclusion.
Passive turned active to bring out a shared term. E.g. 'the budget was raised by the minister' -> 'the minister raised the budget'. Applied to the premise.
A clause turned into a noun phrase (ours, not ATIP's). E.g. 'to be immature is easy' -> 'being immature is easy'. Applied to the conclusion.
A clause turned into a noun phrase (ours, not ATIP's). E.g. 'to be immature is easy' -> 'being immature is easy'. Applied to the premise.
Two wordings judged to be one term (not an ATIP transformation). E.g. 'the obedience of all to the will of one' = 'authority'. Applied to the conclusion.
Two wordings judged to be one term (not an ATIP transformation). E.g. 'the obedience of all to the will of one' = 'authority'. Applied to the premise.

features.name: concepts
features.description: What the argument is about: one or more tags, each `concept` or `concept/sense` for a writer's own sense (e.g. being, being/scotus). Lowercase only. At least one.

features.name: note
features.description: Doubts, the label you nearly chose, or a novel lever written out. The canonical form goes in the subject and predicate fields, not here.

name: webanno.custom.Cue
description: A place that might signal an argument but isn't a connector. Cues that are connectors are Connector spans. E.g. 'who could deny that' (rhetorical), 'namely' (rephrase), 'however' (conflict), 'given that' introducing a stated lever (lever).

features.name: disposition
features.description: What the cue turned out to be.

tags.tag_description: It introduces a stated lever of a connector. E.g. 'given that Socrates is a man', 'as robots are just like us'.
It restates something; no argument. E.g. 'namely', 'that is', 'in other words': 'a bachelor, that is, an unmarried man'.
It attacks a statement; say which in note. E.g. 'but', 'however', 'some say … yet', 'this cannot be, for …'.
Explanation or context; no argument. E.g. 'here nature means the cosmos as a whole', 'after a long winter, …'.
Framing only; its content is kept, the framing dropped. E.g. 'who could deny that …?', 'is it not obvious that …?', 'clearly', 'we are sure that', 'I would argue that', 'you should accept that'.
Undecided; say why in note. E.g. a 'thus' that may be sequence or inference.

features.name: note
features.description: Doubts, the label you nearly chose, or the wording of an implicit statement.
